summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2–3): solving multiplication and division word problems by CHOOSING and using an efficient representation — an array, repeated addition, number-line jumps, or a recalled fact — and recognising whether a story calls for multiplication (combining equal groups) or division (splitting into equal parts), and within division whether it is sharing or grouping. The developmental goal is to move children from counting everything in ones toward using group structure or known facts, and to represent a problem's structure before calculating.
misconceptions: Counting every object in ones instead of using groups or a known fact — not progressing in efficiency.
Not recognising which operation a word problem needs (multiplication vs division; sharing vs grouping).
Modelling with unequal groups and still treating it as multiplication.
Grabbing the numbers and operating without representing the problem's structure first.
Muddling the roles of the numbers (number of groups vs group size) when setting up the calculation.

activities.title: Problem playground: model the story, then solve
steps: Read a contextual equal-groups or sharing story (e.g. '5 bags with 2 apples in each — how many altogether?').
First decide: is this a multiplication story (combining equal groups) or a division story (splitting into equal parts — by sharing or by grouping)? State your choice before solving.
Choose how to model it: build an array, lay equal jumps on a number line, write it as repeated addition, or use a known fact.
Solve and check that your model actually matches the story (equal groups, the right group size and number of groups).

Repeat with a sharing story (e.g. 'Share 15 sweets equally among 3 children'), a grouping story (e.g. '15 sweets are put into bags of 3 — how many bags?') and an array task (e.g. 'Draw an array for 4 × 3').
activities.insight: A word problem's structure (equal groups, array, or sharing/grouping) determines which operation and representation fit; meaning should drive the method rather than grabbing the numbers and operating blindly.

activities.title: Count-all vs known fact: the efficiency race
steps: Take one problem whose total comes from a fact the child knows (e.g. 2×12 = 24, a 2-times fact) and solve it two ways: once by counting every object in ones, and once by using the recalled fact.
Watch the counting-all method work slowly up to the total while the known fact lands the answer at once.
Say why the fact is quicker, and try the next problem using a fact instead of counting all.
activities.insight: For a child who knows the fact, recalling it (or using group structure) is much quicker than counting everything in ones — this efficiency gain is the motivation to leave counting-all behind.

activities.title: Is it × or ÷? Sort and match the stories
steps: Read several everyday stories and sort each one: is it a multiplication (combining equal groups) or a division (splitting into equal parts) situation? For each division story, also say whether it is sharing (number of groups known) or grouping (group size known).
Match each story to the number sentence that fits it (e.g. an equal-groups story to 5 × 2, a sharing story to 15 ÷ 3).
For a tricky pair, explain what in the story tells you which operation to use.
Watch for distractors that combine the two numbers with the wrong operation (e.g. 5 + 2 or 15 − 3).
activities.insight: Recognising which operation a word problem needs — and, within division, whether it is sharing or grouping — is a distinct skill from doing the arithmetic.

activities.title: Market-stall problems: talk through your method
steps: A character (e.g. a market-stall seller) poses an everyday equal-groups buying problem and asks 'how would you work it out?'
Say aloud which operation and representation you would use and why.
Try a follow-up that changes the numbers (e.g. 'If there were 6 bags of 2, how many apples then?') and explain how your method adapts.
activities.insight: Being able to articulate and justify a chosen strategy deepens understanding of why a representation fits a problem.

checkQuestion: Solve these, and show your working with objects, an array, or a jotting. (1) There are 5 bags with 2 apples in each — how many apples altogether? (2) Share 15 sweets equally among 3 children — how many each? (3) Draw an array to work out 4 × 3. (Watch which strategy they choose and whether it fits the problem.)
checkAnswer: 10 apples (5 groups of 2, or 2+2+2+2+2, or the known fact 5×2); 5 each (15 shared into 3 groups); a 4-by-3 array totalling 12 — choosing a fitting representation and reaching the right total.
